rationale:
**The skill text satisfies the requirement, but no test or citation traces to it, and nothing justifies that gap.**

**Content: satisfied.** All four obligations appear in the bundled skills:
- `assets/skills/habeas-requirements/SKILL.md`, "New or changed behavior":
  - It tells agents to draft requirements with full IDs and exact fenced text.
  - It tells them to get the user's agreement.
  - It tells them to keep drafts out of the mdBook while review is pending, and to write no implementation or test code yet.
  - It tells them to install the approved requirements in the mdBook after agreement and only then implement.
- The same section covers revisions: "If implementation reveals a substantive change to an approved obligation, review and install the revised requirement before coding that change." `habeas-evidence` repeats the point: "Review a substantive change to an approved requirement with the user before changing its text."
- `assets/skills/habeas-bootstrap-requirements/SKILL.md` says inferred requirements are proposals. It requires showing the user their IDs and text, and obtaining agreement "before installing them in the mdBook."
- `assets/skills/habeas-evidence/SKILL.md` says "Missing evidence or a truthful false judgment is expected while implementation is pending; do not write placeholder evidence yourself." It also says the supervising agent must not compose evidence JSON.

**Traceability and tests: missing.** A repo-wide search for `requirements_review_skill` finds only the requirement declaration in `md/requirements/cli.md`.
- No `{test}` reference cites it. The only skill-related tests are `tests/setup.rs` and `tests/symposium_hook_smoke.py`. They check that skills are installed and updated, not what the skills say. They cite other requirements such as `requirements.cli.setup`.
- No `{impl}` citation ties the skill files, or the `Cargo.toml` symposium entry, to this requirement.
- No comment explains why tests are absent.
- A simple test could check that the skill files contain the key directives: agreement before implementation, review of substantive changes, user review of inferred requirements, and no placeholder evidence. The tests could not check that agents follow the text. Even so, the absence of any such test is not justified by impracticality.
- No FIXME acknowledges the gap, so `FIXME` does not apply.

name: habeas-bootstrap-requirements
description: Build an initial Habeas requirement set from an existing codebase by tracing its tests and user-visible behavior; use for requirements bootstrapping or coverage audits.
# Bootstrap requirements

Read the project's existing requirements, documentation, public entry points, implementation, and tests before writing new requirements. Follow behavior through the code rather than relying only on test names or top-level dispatch.
Keep two working inventories:
- Every first-party runnable test or test case, including integration tests, doctests, and parameterized cases where present. Record the requirement or example IDs each test checks.

- Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources, including trait declarations, test helpers, and internal helpers. Record its file location and the requirement or example IDs it cites. Also inventory relevant public APIs, commands, handlers, UI actions, configuration, outputs, errors, and distinct observable branches. Do not count one tagged entry point as coverage for deeper code.
Exclude generated and third-party code from the inventories. If a candidate looks user-facing but its purpose is unclear, keep it on the gap list until resolved.

Treat requirements inferred from existing code as proposals. Show the user their proposed full IDs and exact text, along with uncertainty about whether observed behavior is intended or a bug. Obtain agreement on the proposals before installing them in the mdBook; prior explicit agreement to the same requirements counts.

Create or reuse the agreed, stable, chapter-qualified `{req}` requirements in the mdBook. State observable obligations with BCP 14 terms. Group tests that check the same behavior under one requirement; several tests MAY share an ID. For tests of internal invariants, write a requirement for the invariant they actually check rather than inventing a user-facing promise. Distinguish intended behavior from a possible bug or incidental implementation detail.

Put at least one `{test}` reference with a full requirement or example name on each test definition or individual case. A parameterized test can carry a reference at its case source or generating declaration when that is the only editable source. Add multiple references when a test checks multiple definitions. Do not use one file-level tag to stand in for unrelated tests.

Add a requirement or example reference in a Rust comment attached to each inventoried function or method or within its body. An example must cite a requirement, so an example reference still traces the function to a requirement. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions. There is no waiver for an uncited function. If no behavior-specific requirement explains an internal helper, propose an explicit project requirement such as `internal-detail`, get the user's agreement, and cite it. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify unspecified end-user-visible behavior.

Run `habeas author --all` to create requirement and example evidence and each function's attestation in `evidence/rust/<rust_file>.json`. Each assessment has its own model conversation. The harness reviews whole functions against all requirement and example declarations, including ones not already cited, to assess citation completeness. It records delivered source inputs and writes judgments and rationales. The supervising agent must not compose or refresh evidence JSON, determinations, rationales, or snapshots itself, or delegate manual evidence writing to another agent. If authoring configuration or credentials are unavailable, report the blocker instead of substituting hand-written evidence.

Review every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling, when proposing requirements and adding citations. Verify that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and does not introduce additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, cite all of them at meaningful implementation points. For example, a `^C` shortcut needs a requirement that explains why it is accepted. A tag alone does not establish that the behavior matches the requirement. Use the bundled `habeas-requirements` and `habeas-evidence` guidance for directive syntax and the authoring workflow.

The harness assesses whether cited implementations meet requirements and whether tests cover interesting cases, allowing a rationale for absent tests when logic is simple or testing is impractical. For examples, it checks the scenario, test setup, and expected assertions; a true judgment needs a covered `{test}` reference. Its outcomes are true for supported subjects, false for unacknowledged gaps or insufficient information, and `{"FIXME": ["#125"]}` for gaps explicitly acknowledged in source comments or tests. A FIXME does not excuse additional unacknowledged gaps. Function-attestation determinations remain boolean judgments of citation completeness.
For example, source comments can carry these references:
```text
// {test}`requirements.foo`
// {impl}`requirements.foo`

After authoring, run the project tests and Habeas validation. Address reported gaps by fixing source, tests, citations, or agreed requirement text, then rerun `habeas author --all` and the tests. Validation checks evidence without invoking models. Have both inventories independently reviewed against the source and tests before claiming complete coverage. Report test-tag coverage and function coverage as mapped counts over total counts. Claim 100% only when both inventories have no unmapped items and every observable branch has been reviewed. List remaining gaps with file locations and reasons; do not invent evidence or silently exclude difficult cases.

examples, and first-party Rust functions. Current accepted records, including
FIXME judgments, are preserved. Each assessment runs in its own model conversation.
The harness records delivered source inputs and writes the model's judgment and
rationale. The supervising agent must not compose or refresh evidence JSON,
determinations, rationales, or source snapshots itself, or delegate that work to
an ad hoc evidence-writing agent.
Use `--config <name>` to select a saved authoring configuration. Configuration and
credentials stay outside the project. Bedrock defaults to concurrent assessments;
Ollama defaults to one at a time. Each named configuration's positive `concurrency`
setting overrides its default. If the provider reports throttling, lower that
setting and rerun the command. Do not substitute manual evidence creation when
configuration or provider access is missing; report the blocker.
Use `habeas status [<glob>]` to find requirements and examples needing attention,
or `--all` to include accepted records. Use `habeas info <glob>` to inspect their
judgments, inputs, and validation findings. Globs match whole names; `*` matches
any number of characters, including dots. For a focused reassessment, run
`habeas author <full-name>`; add `--stdout` to inspect its JSON without changing
the evidence file.
Address findings by fixing implementation, tests, or source citations. Review a
substantive change to an approved requirement with the user before changing its
text. Every first-party Rust function or method needs its own applicable
requirement or example citations, including trait methods and test helpers; an
enclosing module citation does not cover its functions. When no existing

waiving the function or inventing evidence.
Missing evidence or a truthful false judgment is expected while implementation

name: habeas-requirements
description: Design and vet requirements and examples for user-visible behavior changes in a Habeas mdBook project before coding; maintain definitions and references.
# Habeas requirements
## New or changed behavior

When a user requests new or changed user-visible behavior in a Habeas project, first read the relevant requirements, code, and tests. Identify requirements that already express the intended behavior. For gaps, draft the smallest set of observable obligations, including important outcomes and failure cases, without committing to an implementation.

Run `habeas info <glob>` to read current requirement and named example texts, evidence states, rationales, inputs, and validation findings as Markdown. A full name selects exactly; `*` matches any number of characters, including dots, when you need to inspect a group.

Show the user the full IDs and text of existing requirements to reuse, plus the proposed chapter location, full IDs, and exact fenced text of any additions or changes. State open product choices separately. Ask the user to agree to or revise this requirement set. User-provided exact requirement text or explicit agreement earlier in the conversation counts as approval; a general request to build the feature does not. Keep drafts out of the mdBook while review is pending, and do not write implementation or test code yet.

After agreement, install the approved requirements in the mdBook and confirm their names. Then implement the behavior and add tests and traceability references. Run `habeas author --all` to create or refresh evidence and function attestations through the configured model. The supervising agent must not compose evidence JSON, rationales, determinations, or source snapshots itself or delegate manual evidence writing to another agent. If implementation reveals a substantive change to an approved obligation, review and install the revised requirement before coding that change. Missing or false evidence is expected while implementation is incomplete.
## Reviewing code against requirements

The authoring harness assesses whether a requirement's cited code implements it as stated and whether tests cover interesting design cases. For absent tests, it assesses whether simplicity or impracticality justifies their absence. For an example, it assesses whether test setup and assertions cover the scenario and expected outcomes. Use these criteria while implementing and fixing reported gaps; leave evidence judgments and rationales to the harness.

Requirement and example judgments have three outcomes: `true`, `false`, or `{"FIXME": ["#125"]}`. The harness uses FIXME when source comments or tests explicitly acknowledge the uncovered aspects, recording their issue references or other identifying content. A documented gap does not excuse other, unacknowledged gaps. Use the `habeas-evidence` skill for the authoring workflow.

Inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling. Check that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and introduces no additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, cite every applicable requirement at the relevant implementation point and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A citation alone does not explain why a behavior, such as accepting `^C`, is specified.

Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources needs its own requirement or example reference in an attached Rust comment or within its body, including trait methods and test helpers. Each example cites a requirement. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions, and there is no uncited-function waiver. If no existing requirement explains an internal helper, propose a project requirement such as `internal-detail` for the user's agreement and cite it on the function. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify otherwise unspecified observable behavior.

Every function also needs an attestation in `evidence/rust/<rust_file>.json`. `habeas author --all` creates it by asking the configured model to review the whole function and the requirement and example declarations, including ones not already cited. It judges whether the function carries **all applicable citations** and records the reviewed inputs. Fix missing citations in source, then rerun the harness; do not create attestations or change their determinations by hand.
Function-attestation determinations remain boolean and judge citation completeness, not whether the requirements are satisfied.
## Authoring format

Put requirements in the book's Markdown source directory. Define each with a fenced `{req}` directive: the opening line is three or more colons followed by `{req} name`, and the closing line has at least as many colons. Derive the full name from the chapter path relative to that directory: remove `.md`, change `/` to `.`, and append the directive name. For nested chapters, omit a leading `reqs/` and a trailing `/index` or `/README`.
```text
:::{req} forwarding.quit
Pressing q MUST stop managed forwards.

Everything between the fences is the requirement body, including headings and diagrams. Use a longer outer colon fence when the body contains a nested colon directive. Use BCP 14 terms when stating obligations.

Write a concrete case as a separate `{example}` directive with the same chapter-qualified naming and fence rules. Cite at least one requirement it illustrates from the example body. A true example determination needs test references and an evidence rationale explaining how the tests cover its interesting aspects. Keep names unique across requirements and examples.
Use fully qualified names for implementation, citation, and test references. Place them on the relevant source or book line:
```text
{impl}`requirements.forwarding.quit`
{cite}`requirements.forwarding.quit`
{test}`requirements.forwarding.quit`

When a requirement or example changes, run `habeas author --all`, then the Cargo tests. Address reported implementation, test, or citation gaps and rerun the harness. Validation itself checks stored evidence without inference.
## Shared vocabulary
Use `:::{definition} name` with one nonempty `:phrase: display text` option before
its explanatory body to define shared vocabulary. Reference its chapter-qualified
name with the `{term}` role; the book renders the phrase as a plain link, without
a badge. Names are unique across requirements, examples, and definitions. A
named definition has no evidence record of its own and cannot substitute for a
requirement citation. Dependent evidence snapshots its complete declaration;
review changes to phrases and bodies because they invalidate that evidence.

It MUST direct agents to review substantive changes to agreed obligations with the user. Requirement and example judgments are `true`, `false`, or `{"FIXME": ["#125"]}`.
FIXME means source comments or tests explicitly acknowledge every remaining gap;
the entries identify issues or other source content. The convention is
`FIXME(#125)` or `FIXME(rust-lang/rust#123)`, but other source locations are allowed.
The harness records these references; do not invent issue numbers or change a
judgment to make validation pass. CI accepts true and FIXME only when all schema,

After source or requirement fixes, rerun `habeas author --all`, then
`cargo test --workspace`. Authoring preserves completed writes when another

manifest.replace(current_version_line, f'version = "{next_version}"', 1)

changed_skill.write_text(changed_skill.read_text() + "\nUpdated in the next release.\n")
if updated_sync.returncode:
raise RuntimeError(f"Updated Symposium sync failed:\n{updated_sync.stderr}")
if (skills_dir / skill_names[0] / "SKILL.md").read_bytes() != changed_skill.read_bytes():
raise AssertionError("Symposium kept the old skill after the selected version changed")
